recent_tasks.instruction_summary: Open `~/Desktop/test_files/xlsx/tablebench_0a53ffc65168d29f6a0784ec6741ffb0.xlsx` in LibreOffice Calc. The spreadsheet contains car data with columns: Model, Fuel Type, US gallons

Pivot table creation summarizing data by: Use the `pivot_table` rule type with `load_pivot_tables` utility, comparing `col_fields`, `filter`, `row_fields`, and `data_fields` properties between result and expected xlsx files.
openpyxl exposes pivot table metadata via worksheet's `_pivots` attribute; the `load_pivot_tables` helper extracts field configurations that can be compared structurally.
Pivot table field names and aggregation types (e.g., sum of revenue) are the key properties to verify; positional layout details like exact cell range may vary but field configuration is stable.

Use openpyxl's pivot table structures (load_pivot_tables utility) to compare pivot_props such as col_fields, filter, row_fields, and data_fields between result and expected workbooks on the target sheet; equality of these field lists determines correctness.

When verifying pivot tables in xlsx files, load both result and reference workbooks with openpyxl and compare the pivot table field configurations rather than the rendered cell values, since LibreOffice may store pivot metadata differently from raw cell data.

The 'pivot_table' rule type in compare_table checks the sheet by name (RNSheet2/ENSheet2 pattern), so ensure the pivot sheet exists with the correct name and contains a valid pivot table object with matching field assignments.
Use load_pivot_tables() utility with openpyxl-loaded workbooks; compare pivot_props fields like col_fields, filter, row_fields, and data_fields between result and expected sheets identified by name.

The pivot_table rule type in compare_table checks structural pivot metadata (field assignments), not rendered cell values, so verify via the xlsx pivot cache/pivotTable XML rather than reading cell data with pandas.
Multiple pivot tables on the same sheet are all captured by load_pivot_tables(); ensure each pivot's row_fields and data_fields match the expected aggregation dimension.

Use the `pivot_table` rule type in `compare_table`, which calls `load_pivot_tables` on a specified sheet and compares pivot properties such as `col_fields`, `filter`, `row_fields`, and `data_fields` between result and expected workbooks.
When multiple pivot tables are stacked on a sheet, verify each pivot's field configuration independently; the evaluator iterates all pivots on the sheet and compares their properties as a collection.
Create new sheet with transformed/comput: Use openpyxl or pandas to load the result workbook and check that the target sheet exists by name in the workbook's sheet list before comparing data.

Use pandas read_excel with sheet_name parameter to load the new sheet as a DataFrame, then compare column names (headers) and numeric values against expected; use DataFrame.equals() after rounding both sides to handle floating-point differences.
The sheet_data rule in compare_table uses pd.ExcelFile and DataFrame.round(precision).equals() — replicate this pattern when verifying aggregated numeric columns across sheets.

When verifying SUM aggregations, load both source and result sheets, compute expected sums programmatically from source data, and compare against result sheet values rather than relying solely on a golden file.

The sheet_data rule loads both sheets as DataFrames and calls .equals(), so header row values and all data cell values must match exactly in type and content — ensure numeric aggregation results are stored as numbers, not strings.

When checking a summary/aggregation sheet, verify both the header row labels and the data rows; pandas read_excel treats the first row as column headers by default, so mismatched headers will cause DataFrame.equals to fail even if data rows are correct.

Use openpyxl/pandas sheet_data rule: load the new sheet by name from both result and reference workbooks, round to a fixed decimal precision (default 4), and compare DataFrames with .equals(); percentage change values are floats so rounding tolerance matters.

When verifying year-over-year percentage change calculations, load the sheet as a DataFrame and check that numeric columns match the reference to the specified decimal precision; NaN/None in the first row (no prior year) should also match the reference.

The sheet_data rule with 'RNSheet2'/'ENSheet2' identifiers matches sheets by name across result and expected workbooks; ensure the new sheet name in the result file matches what the evaluator expects.

Use pandas sheet_data comparison (loading both result and reference with pd.ExcelFile) to check that string cells match exactly; INT/TRUNC behavior (floor vs truncate toward zero) can differ for negative values, so inspect the reference file to confirm expected rounding direction.

TEXT concatenation columns that mix cross-sheet references with integer conversion are best verified by reading cell values as strings and comparing against the reference sheet's string values directly.
When verifying a new sheet's column, confirm both the sheet exists by name and that its data rows align with the source sheet's row order.

The concatenated string column stores text values; compare_table sheet_data loads via pandas which reads cell values directly — string equality is checked after rounding numeric columns, so ensure the concatenated column produces strings matching the expected pattern exactly.

When the task specifies 2 decimal digits in the concatenated string, the stored cell value is a string; pandas reads it as a string, so the comparison is exact string equality — verify the rounding and formatting logic matches the expected output precisely.

Use openpyxl/pandas sheet_data comparison (compare_table with sheet_idx using 'RN<name>' and 'EN<name>' patterns) to verify new sheet contents match expected gold file exactly, including headers and row order.
When a new sheet must be populated by cross-referencing an existing sheet against web-scraped data, verify both that excluded rows are absent and that remaining rows preserve correct sort order.
pandas DataFrame.equals() after rounding is the primary comparison; ensure the new sheet's column headers match the source sheet exactly and row ordering reflects the specified sort key.
Read cell data from spreadsheet for exte: Use active_tab_info getter to retrieve the current browser URL, then match against a regex pattern checking for google.com/search?q=<cell_value> to verify the correct cell content was searched.
Use python-docx Document.paragraphs to extract text from .docx files; compare with fuzz.ratio or direct string equality after collapsing whitespace with re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', ...).strip().
The compare_docx_files metric ignores extra whitespace by default (ignore_blanks=True), so minor spacing differences won't cause failures, but exact title spelling matters.
need_rule_judge=True signals the evaluator may use LLM judgment for borderline cases; still ensure the target string is present and correctly spelled in the document.
Use python-docx Document.tables to retrieve all tables in the docx; compare table count, row count, column count, and cell text between result and reference documents.
Cell text comparison should use .strip() to ignore whitespace differences; exact string equality is required for a passing score.
When extracting a subset of rows from a spreadsheet, verify that the inserted table contains only the expected rows/columns and not the full dataset.
compare_docx_tables iterates zip(tables1, tables2) so table order in the document matters; ensure the inserted table appears in the correct position relative to existing tables.
The compare_docx_tables metric only checks cell text content, not visual formatting, so structural fidelity (correct row/column count and text values) is what matters for passing.
When verifying table transfer, iterate every (i,j) cell pair and compare .cell(i,j).text.strip() to catch whitespace differences that would cause a mismatch.

Use fitz (PyMuPDF) to extract text from both the downloaded and reference PDFs, then compare with fuzz.ratio; a high similarity score (near 1.0) confirms the correct PDF was fetched from the spreadsheet URL.
When verifying PDF content identity, fuzz.ratio on full extracted text handles minor encoding differences better than exact string equality.
compare_docx_files uses python-docx Document.paragraphs to extract text, then fuzz.ratio after whitespace normalization; verify the docx contains the correct title string.
ignore_blanks=True collapses all whitespace before comparison, so minor spacing differences in the saved docx do not affect the score.
Use fitz (PyMuPDF) to extract text from each output PDF and fuzzy-compare (fuzz.ratio) against reference PDFs; average ratio across all per-row files gives the score.
When verifying multi-file output, iterate paired (result, expected) PDF paths and aggregate scores rather than checking a single file.
PDF text extraction via fitz page.get_text() captures form field values rendered as text; ensure special Unicode characters are preserved through the PDF generation pipeline.
Output filenames must match cell value strings exactly (including spaces) as read from the spreadsheet column; verify by listing the output directory and checking each expected filename exists.

The evaluator uses the accessibility tree of the email client to verify address-pill labels in the To field; check that email values read from spreadsheet cells appear as address-pill child label elements in the MsgHeadersToolbar To field.
When reading email addresses from a spreadsheet column, use openpyxl or csv parsing to extract cell values; filter rows based on a condition column (e.g., unpaid status) before collecting addresses.
File format export/import/convert: Use compare_csv (line-by-line string equality) to validate exported CSV content against a reference; read both files as text lines and compare lists directly.
Check that the output CSV filename matches the source xlsx basename (same stem, .csv extension) and is placed at the expected path.
Default LibreOffice CSV export uses comma delimiter, UTF-8 encoding, and no BOM; verify the result file's encoding and delimiter match these defaults when comparing against a reference.
compare_csv with strict=True (default) requires exact line-by-line match including whitespace; strip-based loose comparison is available via strict=False option.
Use compare_csv metric against multiple gold variants to handle acceptable output variations; read result file line-by-line and compare strictly or with strip().
Use python-csv or pandas to parse exported CSV; verify column headers and row count match source sheet data.
Use PdfReader (pypdf) to count pages; a correctly scaled export should yield exactly 1 page.
Use fitz (PyMuPDF) to extract text from each PDF page and compare with fuzz.ratio against a reference PDF; scores near 1.0 indicate correct content and layout scaling.
Page-fit settings in LibreOffice Calc are stored in the sheet's page-style; these can be inspected via the UNO API or by checking the ODS XML for <style:page-layout> scale attributes if needed.
When comparing exported PDFs, text-extraction-based similarity is more robust than pixel comparison for verifying content correctness across minor rendering differences.

Use openpyxl.load_workbook to load the result .xlsx and pd.ExcelFile to read sheet data, then compare sheet data (sheet_data rule with RI0/EI0 indices) against a gold .xlsx using DataFrame.equals after rounding.

When verifying CSV-to-XLSX conversion, the sheet_data comparison checks internal cell values (not display formatting), so numeric types, string types, and None/NaN handling must all match the gold file.
compare_table with sheet_data rule uses pandas read_excel under the hood; column headers from CSV row 1 become DataFrame column names, so header presence/absence affects equality.
Check bash_history for a command matching `(soffice|libreoffice).+--convert-to\s+csv` to confirm the terminal was used rather than a GUI export action.

The output CSV must land in the same directory as the source file (LibreOffice --convert-to writes to the current working directory or the directory specified with --outdir); verify the file path matches the expected destination.
Calculated column using formula (arithme: Use openpyxl or pandas to read the computed column values; compare numeric results with expected values using rounding to handle floating-point differences.
Cross-sheet formula results are stored as cached values in xlsx; openpyxl reads these cached values directly without re-evaluating formulas, so numeric comparison works reliably.
Use openpyxl or pandas to read the computed column and compare numeric values against a reference workbook; round to a fixed decimal precision before comparing to tolerate floating-point differences.
When a formula subtracts multiple columns, verify the resulting numeric value rather than the formula string, since different valid formula expressions can produce the same result.

Use compare_table with sheet_data rule and openpyxl/pandas to compare numeric cell values; round both sheets to the same precision (default 4) before equality check to tolerate floating-point differences.

Use openpyxl/pandas to load the sheet and compare the new column's values against a ground-truth file using sheet_data comparison; date values are stored as Excel serial numbers or datetime objects, so use pandas DataFrame.equals() after rounding.
When verifying date-result columns, be aware that pandas may read date cells as datetime64 or as floats depending on the xlsx; normalize both result and expected to the same type before comparing.
The compare_table 'sheet_data' rule with sheet_idx1 referencing the expected file's first sheet ('EI0') is the standard pattern for full-sheet value comparison including new computed columns.
Use openpyxl to read numeric cell values and compare rounded results against expected values; ensure cells store actual numbers (data_type=='n') not strings.
Use the sheet_data rule with pandas DataFrame comparison (rounded to 4 decimal places) to verify computed numeric values match expected.
Verify the new column header string matches exactly using sheet_data or sheet_fuzzy rules.
Bar/column chart insertion: Use openpyxl's chart objects (worksheet._charts) or load_charts utility with chart_props=['type','title'] to verify chart type is bar/column and title string matches the row label; compare against a ground-truth workbook.
Use openpyxl to load the workbook and access the target sheet; iterate sheet._charts to retrieve embedded chart objects.

The 'type' property of a chart maps to the openpyxl chart class (e.g., BarChart with barDir='col' and grouping='clustered' for clustered column); compare against a reference workbook's chart type using load_charts utility with chart_props=['type','title'].
Chart title is stored in chart.title.tx.rich or chart.title.tx.strRef; the load_charts helper extracts it as a string for equality comparison against the expected title string.
When checking chart series data, verify that the series references cover the correct column ranges across all data rows, not just a subset.

Charts embedded in a sheet via LibreOffice are preserved in xlsx format; openpyxl can read them, but chart internals should be compared against a ground-truth xlsx rather than reconstructed from scratch.
Use openpyxl to load the workbook and access worksheet._charts; compare chart type and bar direction (col vs bar) properties via load_charts with chart_props=['type','direction'].
When two charts are required for two datasets, verify that exactly two chart objects exist on the sheet with matching type and direction.
Sheet data equality (sheet_data rule) confirms the underlying source data is unchanged after chart insertion; use pd.DataFrame.equals after rounding to handle float precision.
Line chart insertion: Use load_charts with chart_props=['type','title'] to confirm chart type is line and title matches the row label; also verify the data series range excludes the first column by inspecting series references in the chart object.

Use openpyxl's worksheet._charts to retrieve embedded chart objects; check chart type via the chart object's class or type attribute (e.g., LineChart); the 'chart_props' rule in compare_table checks 'type', so ensure the chart type string matches what openpyxl reports for line charts in xlsx format.

Use openpyxl's worksheet._charts list and inspect chart type via the chart object's class or type attribute; the 'chart' rule in compare_table checks chart_props=['type'] by calling load_charts() which compares chart type strings between result and expected workbooks.
When verifying axis assignments, openpyxl LineChart series references (ser[].val and ser[].cat) encode the data ranges; compare these against expected to confirm correct X/Y column mapping.
SUM/aggregation row with labeled header: Use openpyxl or pandas to load both result and gold sheets, then compare DataFrames with .equals() after rounding to handle floating-point drift; the sheet_data rule in compare_table does exactly this.
When totals can be entered as either hard-coded values or SUM formulas, load with data_only=True (openpyxl) or via pandas ExcelFile to get computed values rather than formula strings.
Check that all expected total cells (row totals, column totals, grand total) are populated and numerically correct — missing cells will appear as NaN in pandas and cause equals() to return False.

Use openpyxl or pandas to read the sheet and verify that a row with a specific label (e.g., 'Total') contains SUM formulas or correct numeric totals for each column; compare internal cell values after rounding.

Use openpyxl or pandas to load the sheet and verify the labeled row exists with correct SUM values across columns; compare numeric cell values with rounding tolerance using DataFrame.equals() or cell-by-cell comparison.
Append rows from external sources: Use openpyxl/pandas to read specific cell ranges (e.g., description, amount, balance columns) and compare with approx numeric matching for monetary values extracted from external documents.
The check_cell rule with method approx:<tolerance> is appropriate for currency values that may have floating-point representation differences; use a tolerance of 0.1 for cent-level precision.
The sheet_fuzzy rule with exact_match on text columns supports ignore_case to handle capitalization differences in manually entered transaction labels.

When transactions are appended, verify both the new rows' individual values (amount column) and the cumulative/running balance column, since errors in one row propagate to all subsequent balance cells.
Use pd.read_excel and df.iloc[-1].astype(str).tolist() to extract the last row as a string list for comparison against expected web-scraped values.
The expected list may be fetched live from the website; compare last row fields positionally (e.g., name, citation counts, h-index, i10-index, top paper title, URL).
Use ignore_case=True list comparison; numeric counts stored as strings must match exactly (no formatting differences).
When verifying URLs appended as cell values, note that the evaluator follows a click chain to resolve the final href attribute, so the stored URL must match the resolved destination link.
Use `compare_table` with `sheet_data` rule comparing result sheet against a ground-truth XLSX; load both with openpyxl/pandas and use `DataFrame.equals()` after rounding to handle float precision.

When the new row's data originates from an external file (e.g., PDF invoice), verify the appended row's cell values match expected amounts, dates, and labels by diffing the full sheet DataFrame rather than individual cells.
File naming pattern conformance can be checked via a `diff` of the saved file against a reference binary, combined with a `check_list` rule asserting the diff output is empty.
When verifying text columns (titles, author lists, URLs), exact string equality is enforced by sheet_data comparison — whitespace, comma spacing, and URL domain all matter.
Sort order is verified implicitly by sheet_data row-by-row equality; descending year sort means most recent year appears in the first data row.
Author list formatting (comma-separated, no extra separators) is checked via exact cell string match in sheet_data comparison.
Create summary/report from external data: Use openpyxl or pandas to load the result xlsx and compare sheet data cell-by-cell against a gold file using DataFrame.equals() after rounding; the compare_table/sheet_data rule is the standard evaluator pattern for this feature class.
When columns contain mixed types (strings, integers), ensure integer columns like attachment counts are stored as numeric types, not strings, since DataFrame.equals() is type-sensitive.
Row ordering matters: verify rows are sorted by the source timestamp/date field (earliest to most recent) since the evaluator does an exact DataFrame equality check.

Use openpyxl or pandas to load the result xlsx and compare cell values against a ground-truth xlsx using sheet_fuzzy rules: header row checked with 'includes'/'ignore_case', data rows checked with 'exact_match' plus leading/trailing whitespace trimming.
For text fields like affiliation/email, case-insensitive exact_match is appropriate; use lstrip/rstrip with space characters to normalize whitespace before comparison.
Sort order verification: read the name column values and confirm they are in alphabetical order by iterating rows and comparing adjacent string values.

The compare_table evaluator's sheet_fuzzy rule supports normalization, ignore_chars, and fuzzy_match (fuzz.ratio threshold) as fallback strategies when exact string equality is too strict for extracted text fields.

Use the sheet_print rule (compare_table with type=sheet_print) to compare printed cell values between result and reference sheets, which handles percentage/string formatting differences better than numeric sheet_data comparison.

When aggregating data extracted from multiple PDF files into a structured table, verify both the row/column headers and the computed values match the reference by loading both as CSV and comparing line-by-line strings.
The postconfig step converts the XLSX to CSV using soffice --convert-to; ensure the CSV path follows the pattern <basename>-<SheetName>.csv so the evaluator can locate it correctly.

When verifying percentage columns formatted as strings (e.g., '12.34%'), the sheet_print comparison via CSV export is more reliable than sheet_data numeric comparison since it validates the exact display format including decimal places and percent sign.

The postconfig step converts xlsx to CSV using soffice with specific delimiter/encoding parameters; the CSV file is then used as the second comparison target alongside the xlsx, enabling both structural and printed-value verification.
Number/text formatting (TEXT/FIXED/decim: The sheet_print rule compares printed (displayed) cell values between result and gold files, so verification should load the CSV or use openpyxl to read the string value of the formula cell and check it contains the number formatted to the expected decimal precision.

Use openpyxl or csv parsing to inspect the formula text in the relevant cell; a FIXED(ref,2) or TEXT(ref,"0.00") formula should produce a string with exactly 2 decimal places embedded in the surrounding text.

sheet_print comparison reads the rendered/printed output of each sheet row-by-row as strings, so any mismatch in decimal formatting in concatenated text cells will be caught; prefer comparing the CSV export for the printed value rather than the internal formula string.

Use sheet_print comparison (compare_table with type=sheet_print) to verify displayed/printed cell values rather than internal numeric values, since zero-padded IDs are stored as text strings and sheet_data comparison may treat them as numbers.

When verifying zero-padded columns, load the CSV export or read cell values as strings; openpyxl cell.value will return a string if the cell is formatted as text, but a number if stored numerically — check data_type=='s' or str(cell.value) to confirm text storage.
Ensure only the target column is modified by comparing all other columns between result and expected using sheet_print or sheet_data rules; irrelevant blank regions must remain untouched.

The evaluator uses `sheet_print` rule, which compares CSV-exported printed (displayed) values rather than internal numeric values — so the cell's number format must produce the correct visible string (e.g., two decimal places shown), not just store the right float.
Use openpyxl `cell.number_format` to inspect the format string applied to cells in the target column; a two-decimal format typically contains `0.00` or `#,##0.00`.
CSV export via LibreOffice `--convert-to csv` reflects the displayed/formatted value, so comparing CSV lines between result and gold is a reliable proxy for verifying the applied number format.
Sort rows by column value: Use the `sheet_data` rule with `compare_table`: load both result and expected sheets as pandas DataFrames and call `.equals()` after rounding; row order is preserved in the DataFrame, so a correctly sorted sheet will match the gold file exactly.

When verifying sort order programmatically, pandas `read_excel` preserves physical row order from the xlsx file, so comparing the result DataFrame directly against a gold DataFrame is sufficient to confirm ascending/descending sort correctness.
Use pandas DataFrame.equals() after loading both sheets to compare row order; openpyxl sheet_data rule confirms cell values match the sorted ground-truth sheet.
Load the result file with openpyxl/pandas and extract the sort-key column values; verify the sequence is non-decreasing (for strings: lexicographic order) by comparing each element to the next.
For alphabetical name sorting, compare full-name strings directly; be aware of locale/case sensitivity issues — case-insensitive comparison may be needed depending on task requirements.
Cell formatting/styling (background/font: Use openpyxl to read cell fill; access cell.fill.fgColor or cell.fill.bgColor and compare RGB/theme values. The `load_xlsx_styles` utility with prop `bgcolor` extracts background colors across all cells for sheet-level comparison.

When comparing bgcolor across sheets, the style rule type `style` with `props: ["bgcolor"]` checks every cell's background color against a gold file — ensure non-target cells retain their original fill (None or no fill) and only target cells have the new color set.
PatternFill type matters: openpyxl distinguishes `patternType` (e.g., `solid`) from gradient fills; a solid red fill requires both correct fgColor and patternType='solid'.
openpyxl cell.fill.fgColor.rgb returns an 8-char hex string (AARRGGBB); compare against the expected ARGB value (e.g., 'FF0000FF' for opaque blue).
cell.font.color.rgb gives font color in AARRGGBB; cell.font.bold is a boolean — both can be checked via _read_cell_style helpers used in check_cell rules.
The check_cell rule type in compare_table supports bgcolor, font_color, font_bold, and value props simultaneously on a single coordinate.
Use openpyxl cell.font.color.rgb to retrieve font color as an RRGGBB hex string; the style rule with props=['font_color'] compares font colors across all non-None cells.
load_xlsx_styles with props=['font_color'] collects font color per cell; only the target cell (highest/lowest value) should have the highlight color, all others default.

When checking font color, be aware that default/unset font color may appear as None, '00000000', or 'FF000000' depending on openpyxl version; compare against the ground-truth file rather than hardcoding.
Sheet management (rename/copy/order): Use openpyxl or pandas ExcelFile to read workbook.sheetnames / sheet_names list and compare exact string equality against expected names; order matters.

Verify both that the copied sheet's data equals the source sheet's data (use pandas DataFrame.equals after loading both by index) and that the sheet appears at the correct index position in the sheet_names list.
Load the workbook with openpyxl/pandas and inspect the ordered sheet_names list; positional index checks are the primary signal for correct placement of moved or copied sheets.
Fill cell values (blank fill / forward-f: Use openpyxl or pandas to load the result sheet and compare cell values in the target range against a gold file; pandas DataFrame.equals() after round() is the standard pattern used by compare_table's sheet_data rule.
When verifying forward-fill correctness, check that previously blank cells now match the last non-blank value above them in the same column, while cells that were already populated remain unchanged.
Cells outside the specified fill range must remain untouched; the sheet_data rule comparing the full sheet DataFrame will catch any unintended modifications to other regions.
Use `compare_table` with `sheet_data` rule comparing result sheet against a gold XLSX; load both with `openpyxl`/`pandas` and use `DataFrame.equals()` after rounding to handle any numeric drift.

When verifying text cell values (e.g., email strings) populated from web lookups, `sheet_data` comparison via `pd.ExcelFile` + `DataFrame.equals()` is sufficient — no fuzzy matching needed if exact strings are expected.
The gold file is fetched from a cloud URL at evaluation time; ensure the result file is saved before comparison to avoid stale data.
Use openpyxl or pandas to read specific cell ranges; apply fuzzy string matching (fuzz.ratio) for address fields to tolerate minor formatting differences.
For phone number fields, strip leading/trailing characters like '+', spaces, parentheses, and hyphens before comparing digits.
For address fields, normalize common abbreviations (e.g., 'Rd'→'Road', 'St'→'Street') before fuzzy comparison.
Use 'includes' match type for phone numbers so that a result containing the expected digit sequence passes even with formatting variation.
Exact match is appropriate for stable fields like restaurant names or headers; fuzzy match with threshold ~85 suits address strings.
Use openpyxl to load the saved workbook and iterate over a specific cell range (e.g., a column slice like sheet['C2:C22']) to extract cell values as a list for ordered comparison.

When expected values allow aliases (e.g., city name variants), store expected entries as either a plain string or a list of acceptable strings, then check membership with 'in' or 'any(...in...)' rather than strict equality.
Verify the number of filled cells matches the expected count before doing per-cell comparison to catch partially filled columns early.
Copy column with header to new sheet: Use openpyxl or pandas to load the result workbook and check that the target sheet exists by name, then compare its DataFrame (via pd.read_excel with sheet_name) against the expected sheet using DataFrame.equals() after rounding numeric columns.
When verifying column copy tasks, check that the new sheet contains exactly the expected columns (header row included) and the same number of rows as the source column, not extra or missing data.
Sheet index notation 'RNSheetX' means result-workbook sheet by name, 'ENSheetX' means expected-workbook sheet by name; use this pattern when the sheet name is known but its positional index may vary.
Add calculated column adjacent to specif: Use openpyxl or pandas to load the result sheet and verify the new column header appears immediately after the target column by checking column order in the DataFrame or worksheet.
Compare full sheet data (all cell values, rounded to a fixed precision) against a ground-truth xlsx using pandas DataFrame.equals(); the sheet_data rule in compare_table handles this end-to-end.
Verify numeric values in the new column equal the row-wise difference of the two source columns; pandas arithmetic on loaded DataFrames is a reliable cross-check without needing formula inspection.
Replace decimal separator in cell values: The evaluator uses `sheet_print` rule which compares the printed/displayed string representation of cells (via CSV export) rather than internal numeric values — use `_load_sheet` on CSV paths and compare line-by-line string equality to verify that numbers display with comma as decimal separator.

When verifying decimal separator changes, export to CSV with a known delimiter (e.g., semicolon) and inspect the text content of numeric cells to confirm the separator character changed without altering the underlying numeric magnitude.

openpyxl cell `number_format` and `value` attributes can be inspected: the internal float value should remain unchanged while the displayed format or cell text should reflect the new separator character.

The `sheet_print` comparison loads CSV exports of both result and expected sheets and compares them as lists of strings, so any difference in how numbers are rendered will cause a mismatch — ensure all numeric cells are consistently transformed.
Multiple embedded charts on same sheet: When a sheet contains multiple charts, load_charts returns a collection; compare the full collection (type + title per chart) against the expected workbook's collection to ensure both chart count and properties match.
Freeze panes: Use openpyxl's `worksheet.freeze_panes` attribute to verify the freeze state; it returns a cell address string (e.g., 'C2') representing the top-left cell of the unfrozen region, or None if no freeze is set. Compare result and expected worksheets' `freeze_panes` values directly.
Cell merge across multiple cells in a ro: Use openpyxl to check merged cell ranges: a cell that is part of a merge (but not the top-left anchor) will appear in worksheet.merged_cells; the `merge` property checked via `_read_cell_style` returns True for non-anchor merged cells and False for unmerged cells.

The anchor cell (top-left of merge) holds the value; verify its value with read_cell_value; verify adjacent cells in the merge range report merge==True and cells outside the range report merge==False.
openpyxl MergedCell objects don't carry values; only the anchor cell has a value, so value checks should target the anchor coordinate only.
Sheet lookup by name uses the 'RNSheetName' prefix pattern in sheet_idx strings (e.g., 'RNSheet2' resolves to the sheet named 'Sheet2').
openpyxl worksheet.merged_cells contains MergedCellRange objects; check that the expected range string appears among them.
For merged header cells, also verify the value is written to the top-left cell of the merged range.
Multi-sheet workbook data modification: Use openpyxl/pandas to load both result and expected XLSX files and compare sheet names list equality before comparing per-sheet data.
For sheet data comparison, load each sheet as a DataFrame with pd.ExcelFile/read_excel, round numeric values to a fixed decimal precision, and use DataFrame.equals() for comparison.

When a task involves reading instructions from an external document (e.g., Writer .docx), the evaluator only checks the final spreadsheet state against a gold file — verify all sheets by index using sheet_data rules across all sheet indices present.
The compare_table metric iterates rules sequentially and short-circuits on first failure; ensure all sheet indices (0 through N-1) are covered in verification.

Use the sheet_fuzzy rule type with range-specific sub-rules: apply exact_match for structured fields (e.g., URLs, IDs) and fuzzy_match with threshold ~90 for free-text fields like paper titles; ignore_case can reduce false negatives from capitalization differences.
Month-on-month growth percentage row wit: Verify the 'Growth' row contains percentage values computed as (current - previous) / previous for consecutive month columns; use sheet_data comparison with rounding tolerance to check computed values match expected.
Time-value arithmetic (multiply time cel: When a cell stores a duration as an Excel/Calc time serial (fraction of a day), multiplying by a plain number requires converting the time fraction to hours first (e.g., =time_cell*24*rate); use openpyxl's read_cell_value or pandas ExcelFile to read the raw numeric value stored in the result cell and compare it with approx tolerance against the expected float.

The check_cell rule with method approx:<tolerance> is the right evaluator pattern for floating-point results derived from time arithmetic; read the cell's internal numeric value (not its formatted display string) to avoid false failures from number formatting.
VLOOKUP formula for cross-table data pop: Use openpyxl/pandas sheet_data comparison: load both result and gold xlsx, read the target sheet as a DataFrame, and use DataFrame.equals() after rounding to verify cell values match; this catches both formula-computed and hardcoded values since openpyxl reads computed values stored in the file.

When verifying VLOOKUP results, check that the filled cells contain the correct looked-up string values rather than formula text; pandas read_excel resolves cached formula results, so comparing DataFrames directly is sufficient without needing to evaluate formulas.

For tasks involving lookup-based cell population, the sheet_data rule type with compare_table is the appropriate metric; it compares internal cell values (post-formula evaluation) between result and gold sheets using DataFrame equality.
Hide rows (row hidden property): Use openpyxl's load_workbook and iterate worksheet row_dimensions; check the 'hidden' attribute on RowDimension objects to verify which rows are hidden. The compare_table 'row_props' rule with props=['hidden'] compares these attributes between result and expected workbooks.
Hiding rows does not delete cell data, so sheet_data equality must also hold — verify both cell values and row hidden flags together.
openpyxl's worksheet.row_dimensions[row_index].hidden returns True/False; rows without explicit dimension entries default to not hidden, so absence in row_dimensions dict means visible.
Duplicate removal / unique value extract: Use pandas DataFrame.equals() after loading both result and expected sheets via pd.ExcelFile to compare cell values; the sheet_data rule with openpyxl/pandas is sufficient for text column comparison.

When verifying order-preserving deduplication, load the target column as a list and check that it matches the expected deduplicated sequence exactly — pandas equals() handles this automatically when comparing full DataFrames.
Ensure the comparison covers the entire sheet (not just the deduped column) so that untouched regions are confirmed unchanged; the sheet_data rule compares all cells including blanks.
Text splitting into multiple columns: Use pandas/openpyxl sheet_data comparison against a gold file; load both sheets as DataFrames and use DataFrame.equals() after rounding to verify cell values match exactly across all target columns.

When verifying split-text tasks, check that the original source column is untouched while new columns contain correctly parsed substrings — openpyxl cell.value reads raw stored values, useful for confirming no formula residue or accidental overwrite.
pandas ExcelFile + read_excel is reliable for sheet_data equality checks; column order and header names matter since DataFrame.equals() is position- and label-sensitive.
Grade assignment using lookup/scale tabl: Use `compare_table` with `sheet_data` rule: load both result and gold sheets via pandas/openpyxl and compare DataFrames with `.equals()` after rounding; this catches both missing and incorrect grade values in the target column.

When a task involves deriving categorical values (grades) from a numeric score using a scale table, verify the entire sheet data rather than individual cells to ensure no unintended cells were modified elsewhere.

Grade columns typically contain string labels (e.g., 'A', 'B', 'Pass'); pandas `.equals()` is sensitive to dtype, so ensure both DataFrames are loaded consistently (same header/index handling) to avoid false negatives.
Sequential numbering with text prefix: Use openpyxl or pandas to read the target column and verify cell values match the expected 'No. N' string pattern for each row; pandas sheet_data comparison via compare_table checks internal cell values, so the text must be stored as strings not formulas resolving to numbers.

When verifying text-prefixed sequences, load the sheet with openpyxl and check that each cell's data_type is string ('s') and value matches the pattern, rather than relying on number formatting alone.
Data validation with dropdown list: Use openpyxl's sheet.data_validations.dataValidation to retrieve DataValidation objects; check .type == 'list' and parse .formula1 to verify the allowed values set (split by comma, strip quotes).

The cell range covered by the validation can be inspected via dat_vldt.sqref or dat_vldt.ranges; acceptable ranges may be a bounded region (e.g., D2:D29) or an unbounded column range — use spreadsheet_range / MultiCellRange comparison rather than exact string match.
formula1 for a list validation is stored as a quoted comma-separated string; compare as a set of stripped tokens to be order-independent.
Verify that the number of DataValidation objects on the sheet is at least as many as expected rules, and that every expected rule is matched by at least one validator.
Matrix transposition: Use openpyxl or pandas to read both the source range and the pasted transposed range; verify that rows and columns are swapped correctly by comparing cell values at transposed coordinates.

The `sheet_data` rule with `compare_table` loads sheets as DataFrames and calls `.equals()`, so the entire sheet content (including the transposed block) must match the gold file exactly — verify placement (top-left anchor cell) and dimensions of the transposed block.

When checking transposition programmatically, iterate over the source range and confirm that value at (row i, col j) in the source equals value at (row j, col i) offset by the destination anchor in the result sheet.
Age calculation from birthdate: Use compare_table with sheet_data rule; load both result and gold xlsx via pandas/openpyxl and compare age columns numerically with rounding.
Age values are typically computed as integer years (e.g., DATEDIF or YEAR(TODAY())-YEAR(birth)); when verifying, read the cell's stored numeric value rather than its display string.
Cells containing date-derived integers compare cleanly with pd.DataFrame.equals; no special date parsing is needed as long as the gold file stores the same integer age values.
Text normalization (whitespace trimming: Use openpyxl or pandas to read cell string values from the target column and compare against expected values; pandas DataFrame.equals() via compare_table/sheet_data rule is the primary check.

Title-case here means capitalizing the first letter of each word and lowercasing all others (Python str.title() semantics); verify that internal whitespace is collapsed to single spaces and leading/trailing whitespace is stripped.
compare_table with sheet_data rule does a full DataFrame equality check, so any extra/missing whitespace or wrong casing in any cell will cause failure — no need for fuzzy matching.
Column reordering: Use `pd.read_excel` or `openpyxl` to load the result sheet and compare the ordered list of column headers (DataFrame.columns) against the expected order; the `sheet_data` rule with `compare_table` does a full DataFrame equality check including column order via `sheet1.equals(sheet2)`.
Numeric unit conversion with formatted s: Use the sheet_print rule (CSV-based printed value comparison) to verify cell text content exactly matches expected formatted strings like '1.2 M' or '3.4 B'; internal numeric values won't capture the string formatting.
When cells contain text formulas combining rounded numbers and unit suffixes, verify via CSV export that the printed representation includes the correct whitespace between digits and unit character.

For half-up rounding verification, note that LibreOffice ROUND() uses half-away-from-zero by default; verify edge cases by comparing printed output against a gold CSV rather than checking formula internals.
The sheet_print comparison loads CSV lines and does case-insensitive string matching, so focus on ensuring the digit-space-unit pattern is consistent across all data rows.
Zoom level adjustment: Access zoom scale via openpyxl Worksheet.sheet_view.zoomScale; note it returns None when at default 100%, so treat None as 100 when comparing.
Use the 'zoom' rule type with comparison methods like 'lt', 'lte', 'eq' against a numeric reference value.
Sheet data integrity should also be verified alongside zoom changes to confirm no cell content was altered.
String concatenation across cells/column: When merging columns from different file formats (xlsx, ods), verify the concatenated values match expected gold CSVs; compare_csv supports a list of expected files so multiple valid concatenation orderings or header styles can all pass.
Open file in LibreOffice Calc from termi: Check ps aux output for soffice process with a terminal tty (pts/ or tty) in the TTY column to confirm the app was launched from a terminal rather than a GUI; use a shell command that greps for [s]office and filters by tty field.
Statistical computation on column with m: Compare result file content numerically using float conversion with a small tolerance (e.g., 1e-4); the evaluator accepts either a bare number or a string containing the number, so check both substring containment and numeric equality.

When computing median after filling NaN/empty cells with column mean, use pandas fillna(mean) then median() pattern; verify the output matches this two-step imputation approach rather than ignoring missing values.
File classification and organization int: Use `ls` on each target directory and compare output string exactly (including newline-separated filenames in alphabetical order) against expected file lists; `exact_match` on `vm_command_line` results is the standard pattern for this feature class.
Add scheduled time slot entry to timetab: Use `sheet_data` rule with `pd.DataFrame.equals()` after rounding to compare full sheet cell values between result and gold files; multiple gold variants (via `conj: or`) accommodate different valid placements of the new slot.

When a timetable uses a grid layout (days as columns, time slots as rows), verify both the label/header cell and the duration-spanning cells are correctly populated by comparing the full DataFrame to a reference.
The evaluator accepts any of several gold files (OR conjunction), so verification should check that at least one valid representation matches rather than requiring a single exact layout.
vm_command_line getter semantics: A vm_command_line getter returns stdout as a string to the rule judge; the rule should parse that result directly and must not run subprocesses or re-open VM paths from inside the judge.
spreadsheet-derived expected values: Do not include a scored rule that only re-reads the source spreadsheet; it can award credit without user output. If deriving expected values from XLSX, use it only as an expected-value helper and avoid optional dependencies such as openpyxl unless guaranteed.
Exact multiline output format: When an instruction specifies exact output lines and order, the evaluator should compare the complete normalized stdout sequence, not just search for labeled counts in any order with optional extra lines.
